And when he had completed forty-six years in the principate, he died.
And in his place arose his son, Jalal {OCR?} al-Din Husayn.
For at the beginning of his rule, this man began to show that he agreed with the faith of the Muslims,
and he fasted and prayed.
And he sent and informed the Caliph of Baghdad,
and Sultan Muhammad Khwarazmshah,
and the rest of the Arab rulers,
that he had turned his face away from the evil ways of his father,
and was walking in the way of Islam.
And when they believed him,
they rejoiced in him and honored him with many gifts and chief presents.
And in that same year, there died also Nur al-Din Arslan Shah, son of Mas'ud, son of Mawdud, son of Zengi, son of Aqsunqur, the lord of Mosul.
For he was just and valiant, and feared by the people of his kingdom as well as by the other kings of his time.
And when his passing drew near,
he made his nobles swear allegiance to al-Malik al-Qahir 'Izz al-Din Mas'ud, his elder son.
And to his younger son,
namely 'Imad
al-Din Zengi,
he gave two fortresses:
that of 'Aqr al-Humaydiyah
and that of Shush,
and their territories.
And he appointed as guardian over his sons his own slave, Badr al-Din Lu'lu',
a formidable and shrewd man, whose character was worthy of kingship.
For when his sickness grew severe, the physicians told him
to go down and bathe in the spring of the holy monastery of Mar Zena, which is on the banks of the Tigris.
And when Badr al-Din brought him down and he bathed,
he was not helped,
because his sickness was unto death.
And while Badr al-Din was taking him up in a small boat to Mosul,
he died before they went up.
And there were only two slaves with them,
and Badr al-Din himself, together with those two, carried him
and brought him by night into his palace,
without anyone else noticing.
And when it was day,
that Badr al-Din remained the whole of that day directing urgent affairs,
and towards the ninth hour he disclosed his death.
And at night he took him out and buried him in the cemetery which he had prepared for himself opposite his palace.
And in his place arose his son al-Malik al-Qahir,
while Badr al-Din held the helm of the political administration.
And in the year 608
